Abstract Introduction Achondroplasia is a rare skeletal dysplasia characterized by severe disproportionate short stature. Vosoritide is currently the only approved therapy. The CrescNet registry is a network of primary and specialized pediatric tertiary centers that aims to improve early detection of growth disorders in Europe. In 2021, an achondroplasia-specific data collection module was set up within CrescNet to enhance data collection among children with achondroplasia and assess the impact of interventions. Here, we describe the module setup and report preliminary real-world outcomes of vosoritide treatment over 3 years. Methods The module was established in 10 of 11 countries participating in CrescNet. Achondroplasia-specific data were collected, including developmental milestones, interventions (such as limb-lengthening surgery, treatment with vosoritide, and growth hormone), complications, and health-related quality of life, alongside standard anthropometric measurements (e.g., height, weight, etc.). Pseudonymized data were sent to the CrescNet central database, Leipzig University Hospital, Germany, for analysis by age and treatment status. Results As of May 2025, 486 participants from 32 tertiary centers were enrolled. Data from 73 untreated and 186 vosoritide-treated individuals with genetically documented achondroplasia were analyzed. In vosoritide-treated individuals, mean height standard deviation score, referenced to an untreated European achondroplasia population, significantly increased from baseline at 1, 2, and 3 years after vosoritide initiation ( p ≤ 0.0001). Conclusion The module facilitates the collection of real-world data to improve understanding of the natural history of achondroplasia and outcomes associated with interventions. Growth data from vosoritide-treated individuals were consistent with clinical trial findings and published real-world data. Longer term follow-up is ongoing. Keywords Achondroplasia Growth Real-world evidence Registry Vosoritide The CrescNet registry is supported by unrestricted grants from BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc., San Rafael, CA, USA, and Hexal, Holzkirchen, Germany. Medical writing support for preparation of the manuscript was funded by BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc. A complete list of the data collected within the CrescNet achondroplasia module is shown in Table 1 . These data are obtained at module entry and during follow-up consultations, as indicated. For children treated with growth-modulating therapies, consultations are held at least every 6 months, but they may occur at longer, more irregular intervals for those not receiving treatment. Both HRQoL and achondroplasia-specific developmental milestone questionnaires are available for participants (aged ≥8 years) or parents/caregivers to complete via a quick-response (QR) code and can be accessed as needed throughout participation in the module. HRQoL questionnaires are filled in at module entry and 1 year after enrollment at a minimum. The CrescNet Achondroplasia Module Data Management System The module’s data management system incorporates a browser-based web application specifically designed to enable efficient and user-friendly data collection. The system features a backend developed in Perl and a dynamic frontend built using JavaScript and the Vue.js framework. It offers interactive input forms for comprehensive master data, along with detailed annotations for diagnoses, phenotypes, genetic information, and achondroplasia-related complications and interventions. To ensure consistency, entries are documented using established standard taxonomies and ontologies ( Table 1 ). Visit data are efficiently captured on a table-like input form that automatically calculates height standard deviation score (SDS), arm span SDS, sitting height SDS, upper-to-lower-body segment ratio SDS, and body mass index SDS based on the selected reference populations (an untreated European achondroplasia cohort [ 24 , 25 ] and a German average-stature population [ 26 – 28 ]). The system also generates graphical representations of growth curves, pubertal development stages, and treatment timelines, with software such as Gnuplot and LaTeX, for insightful data visualization. Users can freely select the reference growth data they wish to visualize, allowing comparison with individual participant data on growth curves. To further enhance its utility, an application programming interface allows external partners to transfer participant data to the CrescNet registry in JSON format. Additionally, the system integrates with REDCap to generate and share invitation links and QR codes with families, enabling access to relevant HrQoL questionnaires. Data collected via questionnaires are automatically linked to the participant’s online record. Data Management, Security, and Quality Control Ethical approval for the CrescNet registry was obtained from the Leipzig University Ethics Advisory Board. Participating institutions enter into a cooperation agreement with the Medical Faculty of Leipzig University, Germany, which regulates joint responsibility for the handling of personal health data. Data collected within the registry are pseudonymized and sent to the CrescNet central database at the Medical Computing Center, Leipzig University Hospital, Germany, for analysis and storage in compliance with the General Data Protection Regulation and institutional guidelines. Each participating institution has access to the data it provides. Access to the online data management system is secured using Transport Layer Security, which encrypts all data transmissions between the user and the server. Each user is provided with a personalized account for the system, ensuring individual accountability and access control. For an enhanced layer of security, the system also offers the option for two-factor authentication. The system is designed to allow individual data to be entered and visualized in real time; its integration with the consultation process supports the accurate input and presentation of participant information. All data quality is assured through review by a pediatric endocrinologist and automated plausibility checks during input that prevent invalid data from being entered. In addition, automatic routines regularly check for abnormal measurement values (e.g., large variations in measurement sequences, unexpected SDS values, etc.), which are, in turn, reviewed by the CrescNet team at least once per quarter. These quarterly screening reports provide an additional opportunity for data verification. Inconsistencies are clarified by contacting the institution that entered data, which is then responsible for updating the record. If important data are incomplete or missing, the CrescNet team will notify project partners to request their support in completing the respective records. Data Analysis For the purpose of this data analysis, only individuals aged <18 years with genetically documented achondroplasia who had not previously entered a growth-modulating interventional trial, received growth hormone therapy, or undergone limb-lengthening surgery were included. Individuals were grouped by vosoritide treatment status (untreated vs. vosoritide-treated). The vosoritide-treated group was further organized by treatment duration: <12 months (all individuals); ≥12 to <24 months; ≥24 to <36 months; and ≥36 months. Individuals were also divided into subcohorts to allow for analysis by age group: 0 to <2 years; 2 to <5 years; 5 to <8 years; 8 to <11 years; 11 to <15 years; and 15 to <18 years. Individuals were included in an age group if they had at least one measurement within that age range; thus, various individuals were represented in multiple age groups. If multiple measurements were recorded for a single individual within an age group, the mean value was calculated. No imputation was performed for missing data points. Collected anthropometric parameters were automatically processed to provide height SDS, arm span SDS, sitting height SDS, upper-to-lower-body segment ratio SDS, and body mass index SDS, as described above. Annualized growth velocity (AGV) was calculated by selecting the closest previous height measurement from approximately 1 year (range: 0.25–1.75 years) earlier; the difference in height was then calculated and divided by the time difference of both measurements. All statistical analyses were performed using R statistical software (v4.2.2; R Core Team 2022). Data were described as numbers and percentages or means and standard deviation (SD). Statistical analysis was only performed if N ≥ 10. Results Participants As of May 2025, 486 individuals with achondroplasia (220 untreated; 266 vosoritide-treated) from 32 specialized tertiary centers across 10 countries were enrolled in the achondroplasia module, of whom 300 had genetically documented achondroplasia and were aged <18 years at module entry. In total, 41 individuals were excluded from further analysis, having previously entered a growth-modulating interventional trial ( n = 9), received growth hormone therapy ( n = 3), or undergone limb-lengthening surgery ( n = 29). Thus, 259 individuals (73 untreated; 186 vosoritide-treated) were analyzed; baseline characteristics across all age groups, grouped by treatment status, are shown in Table 2 . The most common FGFR3 variant across all analyzed individuals was c.1138G>A; p.Gly380Arg ( n = 251). Other FGFR3 variants included c.1138G>C; p.Gly380Arg ( n = 5), c.1144G>A; p.Gly382Arg ( n = 2), and c.1123G>T; p.Gly375Cys ( n = 1). Across all vosoritide-treated individuals, median age at vosoritide initiation was 5.44 years. The analyzed population, including length of vosoritide treatment, is shown in Figure 2 . Anthropometric Parameters In individuals treated with vosoritide for <12 months ( N = 186), mean height SDS ranged from −0.06 (0- to 2-year-olds; n = 177) to +1.60 (15- to <18-year-olds; n = 5), referenced to the untreated achondroplasia-specific population, and from −2.58 in 0- to <2-year-olds to −5.41 in 15- to <18-year-olds, referenced to the German average-stature population. In vosoritide-treated individuals, median AGV was 17.28 cm/year in 0- to <2-year-olds, decreasing to 3.69 cm/year in 15- to <18-year-olds. Across all age groups in the untreated population ( N = 73), mean height SDS ranged from −0.11 (0- to 2-year-olds; n = 60) to −0.20 (15- to <18-year-olds; n = 7), referenced to the untreated achondroplasia-specific population, and from −2.45 (0- to <2-year-olds) to −6.77 (15- to <18-year-olds), referenced to the German average-stature population. In untreated individuals, median AGV was 18.22 cm/year in 0- to <2-year-olds, decreasing to −0.27 cm/year in 15- to <18-year-olds. Mean height SDS was consistently greater across age groups in the vosoritide-treated population than in the same age groups in the untreated population. Complete anthropometric parameters recorded for all individuals, grouped by treatment status and age, are shown in Table 3 . Mean height SDS, referenced to the untreated achondroplasia-specific population, significantly increased from baseline over time with vosoritide treatment; mean height SDS improved overall by +0.51, +0.90, and +1.23 at 1, 2, and 3 years after vosoritide initiation, respectively (all p ≤ 0.0001 compared with baseline), and is shown in Figure 3 . Mean weight SDS, referenced to the untreated achondroplasia-specific population, increased from +0.04 at baseline to +0.53, +0.76, and +0.72 at 1, 2, and 3 years after treatment initiation, respectively. All changes in anthropometric measurements at 1 year ( N = 123), 2 years ( N = 69), and 3 years ( N = 20) post-initiation are shown in Table 4 . Additional data on changes in anthropometric measurements by age subgroups are provided in online supplementary Tables S1–S4 (for all online suppl. material, see https://doi.org/10.1159/000550795 ). Discussion The collection of real-world data for the CrescNet achondroplasia module is playing a crucial role in improving the understanding of the natural history of the condition and determining clinical outcomes in vosoritide-treated and untreated individuals. The achondroplasia module within the CrescNet registry offers several advantages over other registries. First, it offers real-time data documentation and automated data quality control, thereby reducing the likelihood of entered values being incorrect or missing. Its structured format supports the uniform documentation of achondroplasia-specific participant information and, thus, enhanced consistency in data collection. In addition, the module offers a comprehensive view of patient care, allowing contributing physicians to give participants and their families an overview of disease progress and/or treatment response (e.g., by using visualizations to communicate participants’ changes in growth referenced to achondroplasia-specific populations). Furthermore, as physicians are the owners of their institutional data, participation offers research opportunities allowing them to: gain insights into multidisciplinary management, treatment effects, and burden of disease in their own patients by analyzing institutional cohort data; test new research ideas informally; initiate their own registry-independent projects in a research area of interest; and participate in broader registry-related publication projects. The module could be adapted for use in other rare diseases, with likely fewer organizational and procedural burdens than if there were individual registries for different diseases, and advantages in that partner sites would already be familiar with CrescNet data setup, allowing rapid adoption. The existence of the achondroplasia module within European Registries for Rare Endocrine and Bone Conditions (EuRREB) should be acknowledged. EuRREB is dedicated to creating a comprehensive natural history registry for research of rare endocrine and bone conditions [ 29 ]. Similar to the CrescNet achondroplasia module, the EuRREB module collects participant information on family history, anthropometric parameters, clinical features, and therapeutic and surgical interventions [ 30 ]. However, there are notable differences between the two registries. CrescNet has been used for over 20 years as an established online database that allows real-time data entry, easy accessibility, and immediate feedback for contributing physicians. In contrast, EuRREB relies solely on retrospective data entry, which may limit timeliness and completeness. Data transfer between registries is possible from CrescNet to EuRREB, provided an additional participant consent form is obtained but not vice versa. To date, 486 individuals with achondroplasia (220 untreated; 266 vosoritide-treated) have been documented within CrescNet. Although the module collects data from individuals with achondroplasia diagnoses that have been clinically and/or genetically documented, only genetically documented cases were included in the current analysis to reduce possible misclassification. In our study, the untreated achondroplasia population (defined as individuals with no exposure to growth hormone, vosoritide, or surgical limb lengthening) exhibited similar trends in growth to achondroplasia natural history data already published. The height deficit in achondroplasia was apparent in the untreated population, with mean height SDS ranging from −2.58 in 0- to <2-year-olds to −5.41 in 15- to <18-year-olds, referenced to the German average-stature cohort. A similar trend in height deficit was observed in an observational study published by Savarirayan et al. [ 31 ], which was undertaken to collect baseline growth parameters in children with achondroplasia; mean height SDS in children aged <1 year was −2.5 and −3.2 in females and males, respectively, referenced to US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) data for average stature [ 32 ]. As with our analysis, the height deficit increased with age [ 31 ]. To our knowledge, this is the first real-world study to report data on vosoritide spanning up to 3 years of treatment. Our findings revealed improvements in height and height SDS with vosoritide, which is consistent with efficacy data from clinical trials of vosoritide. In a phase 3, randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind study ( NCT03197766 ) with an open-label extension ( NCT03424018 ), height gain in children aged ≥5 years treated with vosoritide for 3 years was 5.75 cm more than in untreated children. Improvements were also observed in height SDS (+0.91 after 4.5 years of treatment, relative to children of average stature) [ 11 ]. Furthermore, in a phase 2, randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind study ( NCT02055157 ) and its open-label extension ( NCT02724228 ), vosoritide had positive effects on height SDS, which were maintained up to 7 years [ 33 – 35 ]. It should be noted that the reference populations used for comparison in vosoritide clinical trials were based on US CDC data for average stature [ 32 ] and an American cohort of individuals with achondroplasia [ 36 ], whereas we used European populations [ 24 – 28 ]. While this may hinder direct comparisons with other studies, the European population better reflects the demographic characteristics of our European cohort and enables more accurate interpretation within our study. Our findings in the vosoritide-treated population were also concordant with real-world effectiveness data for vosoritide. Among 22 individuals who completed at least 12 months of vosoritide treatment in a French early-access program, an increase in height SDS of +0.38, referenced to an average-stature population, was achieved [ 37 ]. Additionally, preliminary data from a cohort of individuals with achondroplasia in Italy ( N = 30) demonstrated a significant increase in height SDS ( p = 0.0006) with vosoritide [ 38 ]. Furthermore, in a retrospective observational study undertaken at University Hospital Cologne, Germany ( N = 34), significant increases in height SDS were observed after 12 months of treatment, referenced to both achondroplasia and CDC average-stature populations (+0.52 and +0.38, respectively; both p < 0.0001) [ 39 ]. In a retrospective cohort analysis in Portugal ( N = 15), mean variation in height SDS increased from baseline by +0.95 ( p ≤ 0.0001), referenced to an untreated achondroplasia population, after 24 months of vosoritide treatment [ 40 ]. Preliminary data also suggest that vosoritide is well tolerated in a real-world setting [ 37 , 38 , 40 , 41 ]. We recognize that our analysis had some limitations. The decision to exclude individuals who had previously participated in growth-modulating clinical trials, received growth hormone therapy, or undergone limb-lengthening surgery was taken to isolate the true effect of vosoritide. The number of individuals in these categories was too small to conduct meaningful subgroup analyses. However, we acknowledge that this approach may lead to a lack of generalizability, particularly as limb-lengthening practices vary across Europe [ 42 ]. Unlike in clinical trials and other real-world analyses, safety and tolerability of vosoritide were not evaluated in our analysis. Additionally, compared with clinical trials with standardized visits, routine clinical practice was variable, leading to visits at irregular time intervals. The 3-year analysis combined children of different ages at vosoritide initiation, meaning it was not always appropriate to report on certain parameters, such as AGV. Small sample sizes within certain age subgroups or specific data elements (achondroplasia-related comorbidities, imaging, surgical interventions, achondroplasia-specific developmental milestones, bone age, and HRQoL) meant that statistical analysis could not always be performed. While we recognize the importance of examining these parameters for a comprehensive understanding of achondroplasia disease burden and treatment impact, our inability to include them at present reflects the current size of the database. However, as the registry continues to grow, longer term data collection will address these gaps. Milestone data are expected to become available within 2–3 years, allowing sufficient time since vosoritide’s approval in infants to assess its impact on development. While changes in HRQoL have already been reported in a clinical trial following 3 years of vosoritide treatment ( NCT03424018 ) [ 43 ], accumulation of a sufficient sample size to demonstrate effects in this cohort will likely require a longer timeframe (approximately 4–5 years). Future analyses will also examine the effect of vosoritide treatment on body proportionality, biological maturation, and other parameters such as lower-limb axis, some of which may be available within the next year. Implementation and utilization of the CrescNet achondroplasia module across our partner tertiary centers are variable. While some centers seamlessly integrate the module into their consultation hours, directly inputting participant data, others face restrictions; owing to local regulations, some partners are unable to access the module at their clinical workstations. In such instances, documentation is presumably stored within local patient data management systems or equivalent internal documentation systems – a detail on which we currently lack definitive information – and subsequently transcribed into CrescNet by a dedicated study administrator. While the implications of local regulations fall outside the scope of the present work, we recognize their significant impact on data entry workflows. Therefore, to gain a clearer understanding of these variations, we plan to distribute a survey among our partner facilities in the future to map their local documentation processes. Additionally, we also intend to explore the user experience of the CrescNet achondroplasia module in future investigations. To do so, we plan to deploy a dedicated user experience survey. Workflow considerations, including the ability of users to input data in real time, must be appropriately accounted for when interpreting the results of the survey. These findings will inform future strategies to mitigate issues such as retrospective transcription errors, through targeted training, for example. Conclusions The CrescNet achondroplasia module has been successfully established, with 486 participants from 32 specialized tertiary centers across 10 countries enrolled to date. The module continues to collect real-world, longitudinal data for untreated, and vosoritide-treated individuals with achondroplasia. Preliminary data from 73 untreated children with genetically documented achondroplasia exhibit similar trends to those already published, while data from 186 vosoritide-treated children with genetically documented achondroplasia indicate that growth outcomes in the real-world setting appear consistent with clinical trial findings and published real-world data. Longer term data collection is ongoing.
